source.title: Why Do You Grok? A Theoretical Analysis on Grokking Modular Addition
source.authors: Mohamad Amin Mohamadi; Zhiyuan Li; Lei Wu; D. Sutherland

record.tranche_reason: The study trains models on modular addition and measures train/test generalization over training, directly testing delayed generalization, though its architectures and optimization setup differ from the original study.
record.gate_note: The paper also gives theoretical results on kernel-regime lower bounds and generalization of low-norm or high-margin solutions. The empirical figures report several curves, but most individual curve values are not stated in the text; those are recorded as figure only. The paper cites grokking results on other tasks, but those cited results are not rows.
record.test_reason: Mainly a theoretical study of grokking on modular addition: kernel-regime lower bounds and upper bounds for low-ℓ∞-norm or high-margin solutions. Its supporting experiments use two-layer quadratic MLPs and a one-layer transformer trained with GD plus tiny ℓ∞ regularization, not AdamW transformers. It addresses the original question with a different method, so T2 rather than T1. Its experiments show grokking curves and an initialization-scale sweep that removes the train/test gap, and they track eNTK change as a lazy-to-rich marker.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that grokking on modular addition comes from a separation between early kernel-regime behaviour, which overfits because of the task's permutation symmetry, and late rich-regime behaviour. In the rich regime, weak ℓ∞ regularization (a proxy for Adam's implicit bias) leads to low-norm or high-margin solutions that provably generalize with far fewer samples. They also note that removing grokking via small initialization slows final generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses modular addition and train/test accuracy, but primarily studies two-layer quadratic networks with gradient descent and explicit ℓ∞ regularization, plus a one-layer transformer. Its regression analysis, optimization choices, and theoretical measurements differ from the original grokking setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization scale changes the size of the train/test gap and can eliminate it; smaller scales make training slower. The study also examines different problem dimensions and regularization settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Permutation equivariance of GD (and Adam) on modular addition implies any permutation-equivariant kernel predictor needs a constant fraction of all data points to beat the zero predictor.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early-phase overfitting in modular-addition grokking is forced by the task's permutation symmetry under kernel-like training, independent of architecture.

record.problems: Most empirical values relevant to the claim are shown only in figures and are not numerically reported in the text. The experiments do not sweep training-set size to measure how grokking delay changes with dataset size. The paper notes that its kernel-regime lower bounds concern ℓ₂ loss and do not establish a lower bound on classification error.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks. No sweep relates delay length to training fraction; Figure 1 right reports only best test accuracy versus train size.
Grokking-like delays on non-algorithmic data (images, text, molecules). Only modular addition is used.
Weight decay (L2) as such, an explicit comparison of the efficiency of generalizing and memorizing circuits, a critical dataset size for grokking under regularization, and ungrokking.
Not tested. The Fourier construction (Prop. 3.8) is a hand-built existence proof, not an analysis of trained circuits or progress measures.
Not tested. A footnote anecdotally says GD did not find Gromov's construction, with no data.
Not tested. Plain or normalized GD is used throughout, and the paper argues Adam's ℓ∞ bias is what matters.

missing.what: Best test accuracy versus training-set size (1.5p^1.5 to 2p^5/3) for p from 113 to 613. The authors read it as empirical support for Õ(p^5/3) sample complexity, which bears on a data-size threshold (V5) and on training fraction (V1).
Classification kernel lower bound (n < Cp² gives at least half the zero predictor's ℓ2 loss). No row records it; the authors note it does not bound 0-1 error.
Cost of removing grokking via small init: training slows, and time to final generalization increases.

record.verdict_notes: Most empirical values are figure-only; states rest on the authors' captions and text. The tranche was changed from T1 to T2 because the setup is GD with explicit ℓ∞ regularization on quadratic MLPs, not AdamW transformers. The eNTK rows were relinked to V3 because they directly measure the lazy-to-rich transition that V3 names. Theorem rows are proofs rather than measurements; they are kept as rows because they are the study's own results.

versions.untested_parts: The empirical results test delayed generalization on modular addition, but do not sweep training-set size to test whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks.
The study does not identify a generalizing circuit forming gradually, memorizing components being removed, or a circuit progress measure anticipating the accuracy jump.

Initialization scale is varied on modular addition. Grokking-like delays on non-algorithmic images, text, or molecules are not tested; weight-norm switching is not separately compared as an intervention.
No realistic LLM pretraining or fine-tuning is studied.

The study analyzes low ℓ∞ norm and sample-efficiency bounds, but does not establish an efficient-circuit mechanism, experimentally locate a critical dataset size, or demonstrate ungrokking below such a threshold.
The study does not compare identifiable algorithms learned across runs.
The study does not test whether adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point softmax limits produce the delay.

rows.check: For V1, the text only says generalization happens above Ω(p²) samples. It never states that test accuracy rises long after train accuracy saturates in the regression runs. Any delay is visible only in the figure, so V1 state is cannot_determine. For V5, this is the regression run where GD with weak ℓ∞ regularization reaches a generalizing solution, which bears on V5.

rows.subject: permutation-equivariant kernel methods
rows.operation_detail: Derived a lower bound on population loss in the kernel regime for modular addition.

conditions.value: n < C p³ for a constant C

rows.measure: Expected population ℓ₂ loss compared with the zero predictor
rows.note: This is a theoretical lower bound, not a measured training trajectory.
rows.check: This is a proved lower bound, not a measurement: kernel-regime methods cannot beat the zero predictor with n < Cp³. It argues that lazy-regime training must overfit, which bears on V3's lazy-to-rich account rather than on V5's weight-decay efficiency account. Relinked from V5 to V3. The subject is a class of methods, not a trained model.

source_check.correct: Zero-predictor population square loss is p. Theorem 3.4 bounds expected population loss below by half this baseline, p/2, for n<Cp³. It does not establish that kernel methods cannot beat the zero predictor at all.
source_check.problem: The row assigns p/2 to the zero-predictor baseline; p/2 is the lower bound, while the baseline is p.

rows.subject: two-layer quadratic network
rows.operation_detail: Proved a population-loss upper bound for interpolating solutions with small ℓ∞ norm.

conditions.value: zero training loss and ℓ∞ norm O(minimum interpolating ℓ∞ norm)

rows.note: A theoretical result: the stated bound applies under the width, interpolation, and norm conditions.
rows.check: A proved bound: interpolating solutions with low ℓ∞ norm generalize with about p² samples. This matches V5's 'low-norm bias favours a generalizing solution' part, but not its circuit-efficiency comparison, critical size or ungrokking. Changed to partial.

source_check.correct: Theorem 3.6 gives Lℓ₂(g,θ*) = O((p²/n)[log³ n + (1/p)log(1/δ)]) × Lℓ₂(Ψ₀), with Lℓ₂(Ψ₀)=p. The conditional low-norm generalization implication is established; circuit efficiency and ungrokking are untested.
source_check.problem: The bound has the wrong power of p and wrong logarithmic expression; partial also treats untested V5 components as an incomplete result.

rows.subject: two-layer quadratic network
rows.operation_detail: Proved a population classification-error upper bound for interpolating solutions with sufficiently large normalized ℓ∞ margin.
rows.uncertainty: with probability at least 1−δ over the training data
rows.note: This bound is conditional on the stated margin assumption; it is not a demonstration of a critical data threshold or ungrokking.
rows.check: A proved margin-based bound, conditional on an assumed Ω(p) normalized margin. It supports only the low-norm/margin-bias part of V5. Changed to partial.

source_check.correct: Observed for the conditional margin-based generalization implication: under the stated width and normalized-margin assumptions, population 0–1 error is Õ(√(p⁵ᐟ³/n)). Efficiency comparisons, a critical grokking threshold, and ungrokking are untested.
source_check.problem: The theorem establishes its conditional implication; missing tests of other V5 components do not establish a partial effect.

relationships.condition: Modular addition, initialization-scale sweeps and eNTK tracking (MLP regression and classification, one-layer transformer)
relationships.reason: Shrinking init scale mitigates and can eliminate the train/test gap (R1, R2). The eNTK barely changes until after overfitting, then changes drastically (R3, R4, R10). Kernel-regime methods provably cannot generalize below a constant data fraction (R11). This is consistent with a lazy-to-rich switch.
relationships.display_finding: Smaller initialization reduced or eliminated the training–test gap, the empirical neural tangent kernel changed substantially only after overfitting, and kernel methods provably failed below a constant data fraction.

relationships.condition: Theory plus GD with ℓ∞ (not L2) regularization on modular addition

relationships.display_finding: Theory established generalization with far fewer samples under low-norm or high-margin bias, and gradient descent found low-norm weights under ℓ∞ regularization.

tranche.reason: The study addresses delayed modular-addition generalization using kernel lower bounds, conditional generalization theory, and quadratic networks trained with explicitly ℓ∞-regularized GD.

source_check.notes: The kernel lower bounds concern square loss; the paper explicitly leaves classification-accuracy lower bounds open. Eliminating the train–test gap through smaller initialization slows final generalization.

statements.problem: The factual description is accurate, but limits_scope is unsupported: omitted efficiency and ungrokking tests are not evidence against those components.
